```{r}
set.seed(123)
S <- 100000
alpha_post <- 476
beta_post <- 526
theta_samples <- rbeta(S, alpha_post, beta_post)
```

# (2)
```{r}
mean(theta_samples)
var(theta_samples)
quantile(theta_samples, c(0.025, 0.975))
```
The post mean is 0.475098707405117, posterior variance is 0.000248366426453703, 95% posterior interval is [0.4441427, 0.5060320].


# (3)
```{r}
post_mean <- mean(theta_samples)
post_var <- var(theta_samples)
hist(theta_samples, breaks = 50, prob = TRUE, 
     main = expression(paste("Posterior Distribution of ", theta)),
     xlab = expression(theta))
curve(dnorm(x, mean = post_mean, sd = sqrt(post_var)), add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```
Yes, it looks like normal distribution, because we have n=1000, which is very large

# (4)

```{r}
lambda_samples <- -log(theta_samples) + log(1 - theta_samples)

hist(lambda_samples, breaks = 50, prob = TRUE, 
     main = expression(paste("Posterior Distribution of ", lambda)),
     xlab = expression(lambda))
```

```{r}
mean(lambda_samples)
var(lambda_samples)
quantile(lambda_samples, c(0.005, 0.995))
```
The posterior distribution of lambda looks like a Gaussian distribution. The mean is 0.0997873, variance is 0.0040017, and the 99% posterior interval is [-0.06309092, 0.26245380].

# (5)
```{r}
mean(theta_samples < 0.485)
```

73.44% data support the claim that the proportion of female births in the
population of placenta previa births is less than 0.485

# (6)
Beta(9+1, 20-9+1) = Beta(10, 12)
```{r}
theta_samples_small <- rbeta(S, 10, 12)
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
hist(theta_samples, xlim=c(0,1), main="n=1000 (Large Data)")
hist(theta_samples_small, xlim=c(0,1), main="n=20 (Small Data)")
```
```{r}
mean(theta_samples_small)
var(theta_samples_small)
quantile(theta_samples_small, c(0.025, 0.975))
```
The data for 20 births became much more unstable, the posterior variance increased from 0.0002483664 to 0.01081704, and then the 95% posterior interval became a much larger range, from [0.4441427, 0.5060320] to [0.2568797, 0.6599812]. The histogram became wider, not concentrate enough. We can't conclude anything since the outcome is affectted too much by randomness.
